title: Can equilateral and isosceles triangles be right or obtuse?
description: An equilateral triangle has three equal angles of sixty degrees, so it can be neither right angled nor obtuse angled. An isosceles triangle with a right angle or an obtuse angle between its equal sides is built and its other angles are found.
teaching_notes: One idea: equal sides bring equal angles, and the angles add up to one hundred and eighty. Watch for students who think an equilateral triangle could be stretched into a right angle.

source: Through construction, explore if it is possible to construct an equilateral triangle that is (i) right-angled (ii) obtuse-angled. Also construct an isosceles triangle that is (i) right-angled (ii) obtuse-angled.
video_script.why: The child can name a triangle by its sides and by its angles, and now asks which pairs of names can go together.
video_script.substitution: Use equal sides to get equal angles, then divide one hundred and eighty by three for the equilateral triangle, and take the large angle away from one hundred and eighty and halve what is left for the isosceles ones.
video_script.anchor: an equilateral triangle and two isosceles triangles with their angles marked
video_script.payoff_line: An equilateral triangle can be neither, but an isosceles triangle can be both

final_answer.value: (i) and (ii): not possible for an equilateral triangle; an isosceles triangle can be right-angled (90°, 45°, 45°) or obtuse-angled (120°, 30°, 30°)
final_answer.spoken: an equilateral triangle can be neither, but an isosceles triangle can be both

maths_rules: equal sides give equal angles (a paper fold puts the matching angles on each other)
equilateral: three equal angles, each 180° ÷ 3 = 60°, which is less than 90°, so it is never right-angled or obtuse-angled
isosceles right-angled: 90° between two equal sides of 4 cm; the other two angles are equal and add up to 180° - 90° = 90°, so each is 90° ÷ 2 = 45°
isosceles obtuse-angled: 120° between two equal sides of 5 cm; the other two angles are equal and add up to 180° - 120° = 60°, so each is 60° ÷ 2 = 30°
video_script.design: An equilateral triangle and two isosceles triangles are drawn in the anchor band. A paper fold shows the matching angles, and the working finds the angles in turn.

beats.on_screen: Answer: equilateral: neither;  isosceles right-angled: 90° ÷ 2 = 45°, so 90°, 45°, 45°;  isosceles obtuse-angled: 60° ÷ 2 = 30°, so 120°, 30°, 30°

marks.right: 90° ÷ 2 = 45° is written and the angles 90°, 45°, 45° are marked

narration: <bookmark mark='ans'/>An equilateral triangle can be neither, but an isosceles triangle can be both.
<bookmark mark='right'/>Half of ninety is forty five, so the right angled one has ninety, forty five and forty five.
<bookmark mark='obtuse'/>Half of sixty is thirty, so the obtuse angled one has one hundred and twenty, thirty and thirty.
<bookmark mark='check'/>Check, both sets of angles add up to one hundred and eighty.
